newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish economy to grow for fourth year - ESRI says.
newsitem.headline: Irish economy to grow for fourth year - ESRI says.

text.p: Ireland should see a fourth successive year of rapid non-inflationary growth in 1977 and expansion of output and employment could continue for several more years, a leading research body said on Friday.

But the Economic and Social Research Institute warned that if sterling did not start to depreciate soon, Irish authorities would have to consider how to lower the Irish pound's value in the run-up to the singe Euro currency.
The ESRI said it estimated that real Gross National Product few by about 6.5 percent in 1966 with a rapid rise in employment and consumer price inflation averaging 1.6 percent.
It predicted an increase in real GNP this year of about 5.5 percent with a less marked rise in exmployment and inflation remaining below two per cent.

"Thus 1977 is expected to be the fourth successive year of rapid non-inflationary growth in the Irish economy and the prospects are that the virtuous circle of output and employment growth, improving public finances and low inflation can continue for several more years, " it said.
The ESRI said sterling's strength against continental European countries since mid-1966 posed "a potential policy difficulty in approach to EMU.

For reasons of competitiveness and exposure to the risk of a future sterling depreciation, it would be undesirable to "lock the Irish pound into monetary union at its current value against the major continental currencies," it said.

By following a path of moving between sterling and the German mark, the value of the Irish currency has significantly improved Irish competitivness against Britain but weakened Irish competitiveness against continental Europe, it said.

Even without EMU, the current situation would not be comfortable and the prospect of further Irish pound appreciation against continental currencies because of a unilateral rise in Irish interest rates could "not be contemplated with equanimity," it said.
The imminence of EMU will increase the likelihood of European currency instability between now and the end of 1988, it forecast.
The ESRI said Irish authorities "must take a view" on the rate of exchange at which individual countries will be locked into EMU.
It would not be desirable for the Irish pound to be locked into EMU at anything close to currency exchange rates, the institute said.
An entry rate at or close to the existing ERM central rate of about 2.41 marks would be much more appropriate in terms of competitiveness and limiting long-term sterling risk, it said.
The institute said the issue could resolve itself in coming months depending on market trends and the decision on how and where to set rates.
"However, were sterling to remain strong or to appreciate further, significant transition problems could arise."
It said the UK currency was over-valued in relation to production costs and growth potential and these would eventually lead to sterling depreciating against continental currencies.
But this was unlikely to happen soon.
A depreciation of the Irish pound against continental currencies, sterling and the dollar simultaneously would almost certainly result in a once-off rise in Irish inflation in 1998 and 1999, it said.
"This would appear to be a worthwhile price for avoiding entering monetary union with an overvalued currency," it said.
